name: Umar Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good morning, Umar, thanks for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you share is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a big hydraulic excavator at the phosphate mine, loading trucks at the face, and I lead the excavator crew on days. I start at six with the pre-start checks, then it's load, swing, dump, all day, while I keep an eye on the younger operators over the radio. I love getting the bucket fill just right, three passes and the truck's full. What wears me out is the pay, because this mine sits in the lower wage zone and we earn less than the same job on the coast.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Efua does hair from a room in our house, so her income goes up and down. We have two boys, eight and thirteen, and a mortgage on a house near the mosque. We keep maybe two weeks of money in the bank, never more. Outside the mine, there's farming and the town council, that's it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use an AI assistant to study for my next licence, to do the books for Efua's business, and to plan the boys' football club schedule. Last year I used it to teach myself how to quote small earthmoving jobs, and I've done a few on weekends with a hired mini-digger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now people can stop panicking and get back to work. I'd say the tools that work, keep them, and the hype, forget it. I'd say that at Friday prayers if anyone asked, and in the football parents' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, because I've been getting ready for big change and I like the tools. But it also means my job's safe and my weekend digging grows slowly. I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at the mine and grow the weekend earthmoving, maybe one more job a month. I'd keep using the AI to study and do the books. And put a bit more aside, even fifty a month, so we're not two weeks from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady, like a normal week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the weekend digging. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farmer at the mosque needed a drainage trench and couldn't get anyone. I hired a mini-digger for the Saturday, asked the AI how to price it, and he paid me on the spot. Now I've done eleven jobs, mostly drains and driveways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the mine know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My supervisor knows, he even sent me one job. As long as I'm sharp on Monday, nobody minds. A man who works for himself on the weekend works harder for you on the weekday, that's what I tell him.

S0.say: I'd say people can stop panicking and get back to work, keeping the tools that work and forgetting the hype. I'd say it at Friday prayers or in the football parents' group if asked.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a little disappointed, because I've been preparing for big change and like the tools. But my job stays safe and my weekend digging can grow slowly, which I can live with.
S0.do: Keeps working at the mine and adds about one weekend earthmoving job a month. Keeps using AI to study and do the books, and saves about fifty a month.
S0.quote: A man who works for himself on the weekend works harder for you on the weekday, that's what I tell him.
S0.fieldNote: Umar is already building a small business on the side using AI to learn pricing. He ties work to faith and community, through the mosque and football club. A plateau suits him fine, though he'd be slightly disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming, so stop complaining and start learning. Nobody owes us a job, but a good company trains its people, and a good worker takes the training. I'd tell the young operators that straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's a chance. The excavators will go semi-autonomous, and someone has to supervise them and fix the problems, and I'm good with both machines and the AI. And outside the mine, farmers will want someone who can bring in a small robot digger and handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the first automation training at the mine. I'd use the AI to write a proper plan for the earthmoving business and talk to the bank about a small loan for a second-hand mini-digger, maybe fifteen thousand. And Efua and I would keep spending tight while I do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Interested. A little nervous about the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a small loan. With two weeks saved, isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, I won't pretend. But hiring the digger costs me a third of every job. If I own one, the jobs pay it off in two years, and I've done the sums three times. Efua made me do them a fourth time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My crew's young ones, the ones who only play games on their phones and think that's technology. And old Kwame, who's been on the excavator thirty years and won't touch a tablet. I'd try to bring Kwame onto my weekend jobs, he's the best operator I know.

S1.say: I'd say change is coming, so stop complaining and start learning, because nobody owes us a job. A good company trains its people and a good worker takes the training, and I'd tell young operators that straight.
S1.think: Honestly I think it's a chance: excavators go semi-autonomous and someone has to supervise and fix them. Farmers will also want someone to bring in and handle a small robot digger.
S1.do: Volunteers for the mine's first automation training. Writes a business plan with AI and asks the bank for a loan of about fifteen thousand for a second-hand mini-digger, while keeping household spending tight.
S1.feel: Calm and interested, a little nervous about the loan.
S1.quote: If I own one, the jobs pay it off in two years, and I've done the sums three times. Efua made me do them a fourth time.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like opportunity to Umar, both inside the mine and in his side business. He is willing to borrow despite thin savings, but is honest about the risk. He thinks of older colleagues and would bring them onto his own jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for families to adjust, and the companies should give people time and training. I don't want handouts, but I'd want the rules to make companies do right by their workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even supervising the machines goes quickly, and a robot digger can do a farmer's trench too. My whole plan assumed some years. With two weeks in the bank, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the digger loan, because I can't borrow against work that might disappear. I'd take every automation shift the mine offers and save every extra dollar. And I'd look at buying a small robot digger with a partner from the mosque, so we own the machine instead of competing with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach's tight, but I'm still thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Owning the machine with a partner. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots dig the trenches, someone still owns the robot and finds the customers. Yusuf, who runs the hardware shop, has some savings and I have the know-how. It's a gamble, but it's better than sitting and waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your boys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to work hard, pray, and learn how these machines think, not just how to use them. My thirteen-year-old already asks the AI more questions than I do. I'd tell him to keep asking.

S2.say: I'd say two years is too fast for families to adjust and companies should give time and training. I don't want handouts, but I'd want rules making companies do right by workers.
S2.think: I think even supervising machines goes quickly, and a robot digger could do a farmer's trench too. My plan assumed some years, so with two weeks in the bank it's frightening.
S2.do: Holds off on the digger loan and takes every automation shift the mine offers, saving every extra dollar. Explores buying a small robot digger with a partner from the mosque so they own the machine rather than compete with it.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight stomach, but still thinking.
S2.quote: If robots dig the trenches, someone still owns the robot and finds the customers.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture threatens Umar's whole timeline, yet he stays inventive rather than frozen. His free-market instinct shows in his plan to own the robot rather than fight it. He'd still turn to his faith community for a business partner, not to government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to work, so get started now. I'd say the companies should back apprenticeships and the town should back its own businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me three or four good years at the mine supervising automation, and time to build the weekend business into something real. The end point still worries me, but I'd have a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the automation training in year one and buy the second-hand mini-digger in year two, once I'd saved a deposit. By year three I'd want a small robot digger on the books. And I'd set up a simple company with Efua doing the accounts, since she already runs her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to build all that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some Saturdays with the boys, which I don't like. I'd take the older one with me on jobs, so he learns. Sunday is family, that doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe leaving the crew. They'd see me going off on my own and think I'm abandoning them. I'd try to hire some of them as the business grew, Kwame first.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to work, so get started now. Companies should back apprenticeships and the town should back its own businesses.
S3.think: I think five years gives me three or four good years supervising automation and time to make the weekend business real. The end point still worries me, but I'd have a head start.
S3.do: Takes automation training in year one, buys a second-hand mini-digger in year two once he has a deposit, and aims to own a small robot digger by year three. Sets up a company with Efua handling the accounts.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.
S3.quote: They'd see me going off on my own and think I'm abandoning them.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Umar build in sensible steps without risky borrowing. His only regret would be seeming to abandon his crew, and he plans to hire them. Family time on Sundays is fixed, consistent with his values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it can't blame the machines. I'd be telling the young ones to learn a skill and start something on the side now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years is good for me. I'd be fifty-three with my own small business, the boys grown, and the mortgage much smaller. I'd be one of the people running the robots, not one of the people replaced by them, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the automation training, buy the mini-digger in year two, and grow slowly, no big loans. By year five I'd want two machines and one employee, by year eight maybe a robot unit. And I'd teach a free Saturday class at the mosque hall on using AI for small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who wastes it can't blame the machines. Isn't that a bit hard on people like Kwame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it is. Kwame is fifty-five and he's given thirty years. I'd say it differently to his face, and I'd help him. But for the young ones, I stand by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies with big robot fleets could undercut a small man like me. That's the market, I can't complain about it. I'd just have to be the one the farmers know and trust.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and anyone who wastes it can't blame the machines. I'd tell the young operators to learn a skill and start something on the side now.
S4.think: I think ten years is good for me: at fifty-three I'd have my own small business, grown boys and a smaller mortgage. I'd hope to be running the robots, not replaced by them.
S4.do: Takes the automation training, buys a mini-digger in year two and grows without big loans, aiming for two machines and an employee by year five and a robot unit by year eight. Teaches a free Saturday class on AI for small business at the mosque hall.
S4.quote: I'd just have to be the one the farmers know and trust.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years suits Umar completely, and he sounds hopeful. When challenged about older colleagues he softened his tough line for them but kept it for the young. He accepts market competition from big fleets as fair.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my plan needs time and we've got two weeks in the bank. What would help is small business loans that don't need a big deposit, for workers starting something of their own, and companies giving their people first chance at the new jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the young ones. The thirteen-year-olds now will finish school right when this lands. I worry more about my son than about me.

headlineQuote: I'd be one of the people running the robots, not one of the people replaced by them, God willing.
portrait: Umar Mensah is a 43-year-old excavator crew lead at a phosphate mine in a low wage zone, married to a home hairdresser, with two sons, a mortgage and about two weeks of savings. He uses AI every day and has taught himself to run weekend earthmoving jobs with a hired mini-digger. He stays calm through the plateau and steady change, seeing a chance to supervise automation and own his own machines, and becomes anxious only when two years cuts his timeline short. A man of faith who wants no handouts, he plans with five or ten years to build a small business that owns robots rather than competes with them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his plan needs time and the family has only two weeks of money in the bank.
whatWouldHelp: Small business loans without a big deposit for workers starting their own firms, and companies offering their staff first chance at new jobs.
